title: Tom Davidson: the speed-up may not be mostly money
who: Tom Davidson, senior research fellow at Forethought. Thread on X, 15 November 2026, with a reply from Alex Imas the same day.
claim: Garicano and Imas conclude that the faster progress at Anthropic is mostly explained by faster growth in research spending, so we are no closer to an explosion. Davidson argues this rests on how much research Anthropic is assumed to have had before 2024. Using the spending in Anthropic's filings, he finds cumulative spending grew about 3.3 times a year before October 2025 and 4.4 times after, while progress went from about 15 to 29 points a year. So each doubling of cumulative spending bought more progress than before: about 9 points, then about 14. On that reading, returns to research rose, which is a step towards the threshold. In his figures, φ rises from about 0.45 to 0.65.
kind: A re-analysis of Garicano and Imas's model with different starting figures. No new data.
questions: How much of the speedup is money, and how much is AI? Are ideas getting harder to find in AI?
caveats: Davidson says he may have missed something. Imas replied that the right starting figure is not what Anthropic spent but the cumulative research behind everything it began with, including what it inherited from the field, and that this cannot be read from the filings. Their fits put it at $1.0 to $2.1 billion. Near $2 billion, returns look the same before and after October 2025; nearer $1 billion, either returns rose or productivity jumped once. Imas agreed the paper should have been clearer about this.
fits: It turns the question on this site into one about a single assumption: how much past research Anthropic was building on in early 2024. It bears directly on Fiddling with ASI, whose settings come from Garicano and Imas's fits; Davidson points out that their separate before-and-after fits let that starting figure reset between periods. The spending puzzle explains why spending figures alone cannot separate rising returns from a one-time jump.
tag: Claimed. A disagreement about one input to the model, with both sides' figures shown.

title: Dwarkesh Patel: the case that AI research will soon automate itself
who: Dwarkesh Patel, podcaster and writer. ‘The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development’, essay with an appendix, 13 November 2026.
claim: His median year for automated researchers to match the best human AI researchers is 2028, assuming labs do not intentionally slow down; he gives a 25% chance this happens after 2032. He expects AI at least as good as top human experts in every field by 2030, possibly sooner. His reasons: AI already speeds up AI research; in fields where answers can be checked, such as maths, AI went from weak to beyond the best humans within a few years; and most of AI research can be checked too, through training results, test scores and efficiency. Once research is automated, he sets AI improving its own research against ideas getting harder to find. If AI wins, he expects a ‘software-only singularity’; if difficulty wins, a ‘spark’ of three to six years of progress in one year, then a slowdown until more computing is built. He calls the two equally likely.
kind: An argument with forecasts, drawing on figures published by METR and the labs. No new data.
questions: Is AI starting to do its own research? What would an explosion need, and what would we see first?
caveats: He gives a 25% chance that full automation comes after 2032, mainly because AI may still be unable to learn on the job. He grants that experiments, data and choosing what to measure are real bottlenecks that make the fastest takeoff less likely. His probabilities are personal judgements.
fits: The strongest case for an explosion on this page, and the closest to its framing: stories 4 and 5 in Fiddling with ASI show the shape of his two outcomes, though story 4's spark is smaller than his. It answers Chalmers directly, arguing that research judgement can partly be checked and trained; Toby Ord, whom he quotes, doubts that AI can yet ask the deep questions. It supplies the half our research machine leaves out: the machine works out how much research labour holding the pace would need, and Dwarkesh argues AI researchers will supply it. Like Garicano and Imas, he notes that labs must roughly quadruple their research computing each year just to hold the pace. Where Garicano and Imas find no clear sign yet of AI feeding its own research in the public data, his evidence is what the labs report from inside.
tag: Claimed. A forecast built on an argument. We checked four figures he cites against their sources: METR's guess that about 80% of Anthropic's October 2026 speedup came from AI, which METR calls subjective; Anthropic's report that Claude ‘leads’ 26% of its AI research work as of August 2026, up from under 1% in February, where ‘leads’ means completing most of a task end to end while a human supervises; OpenAI's report that its 90th-percentile researcher uses more than $7,000 of AI tokens a day; and OpenAI's report that its agents found a proof for the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem about 88 hours after the first agents started, followed by about 17 more hours for formalization and verification in Lean. OpenAI researchers directed groups of agents, moved resources between problems and shared intermediate findings; the Navier–Stokes work used about 130 billion output tokens. We did not check his other figures.

title: Luis Garicano and Alex Imas: what more data shows
who: Luis Garicano and Alex Imas, economists. ‘Are we approaching an intelligence explosion?’, Silicon Continent, 13 November 2026, with an online appendix.
claim: Using Anthropic's filings, METR's chart and their own staff estimates: progress per dollar fell about 69% and per technical employee about 38%. Fitting a standard model of research to sixteen model scores, more inputs explain part of the speedup (at most about half, in their most generous version) and the rest looks like a one-time jump in research effectiveness. On their model, ideas are getting harder to find, at a similar rate before and after October 2025; that rests on their assumptions, and the estimates are imprecise. No clear sign yet of AI supplying research input that grows with capability.
questions: How much of the speedup is money, and how much is AI? Are ideas getting harder to find? Is AI starting to do its own research?
fits: The fullest analysis of the spending puzzle we have found. Its broad reading sits near Krier's, with a one-time boost that the per-dollar chart could not show. It does not contradict METR's guess about AI's share, which concerns a later date.
tag: Claimed. Arithmetic checked against the filings; the model was not refitted by us.
caveats: Staff numbers are their estimates from published shares; the final score falls inside their effort-only forecast's margin of error; the most generous jump estimate is not statistically clear; with a one-year research delay the per-dollar fall shrinks from about 69% to about 40% (from 64% to 10% in a January-to-September comparison); in their broadest test of measurement error, about one in eleven re-runs of their model meet its explosion condition, which is not a probability, independent of their model, that one has begun; results are model comparisons, not measured effects of AI tools. Their appendix says they worked with Gemini Carbon, Fable 5.2 and Astra.

title: David Chalmers: the ‘factor F’ question
who: David Chalmers, philosopher. Post on X, 11 November 2026, with replies to 12 November.
claim: Several researchers read METR's 2x speedup as support for an intelligence explosion around 2027. Chalmers asks how that reasoning works. He describes the main rival view, which he calls the "factor F hypothesis", and says he does not know whether it is true: there is at least one capacity F (he suggests creativity, research vision or planning) that an AI must have to reach superhuman research, and that is hard enough to build that leading systems will not have it soon. The 2x speedup, he says, reflects gains in other capacities G, such as coding and experiments, where the speedup may be larger, perhaps 10x. Under the F hypothesis, G can explode on its own and give an "intelligence subexplosion" below general intelligence. He does not see why the speedup makes the F hypothesis much less likely. Routes from 2x to an explosion in 2027 need "huge premises", such as extrapolating ever-faster speedups. He adds that he is worried about near-term superintelligence all the same.
kind: An argument about what the evidence shows. No new data.
questions: Is AI starting to do its own research? What would an explosion need?
fits: It gives a name to a gap the economics leaves open. Garicano and Imas find a one-time jump in research effectiveness "consistent with" coding agents. Chalmers's picture would predict gains of that kind if they come in G and not F. He also allows that G could improve itself fast, a "subexplosion" below general intelligence. The research machine cannot show this directly: its σ setting is about research labour against computing, not about one research skill against another. Chalmers's F is a bottleneck of the second kind. Replies push back. Daniel Kokotajlo: many candidate Fs have been proposed before and overtaken quickly. One reply suggests strong G could let AI build F itself, and Chalmers grants the point. Peli Grietzer offers a reading Chalmers endorses: METR's report is evidence for "if general ASI is coming soon then general ASI is coming very soon".
tag: Claimed. An argument about what the evidence shows; no new data.
